subject: Climate & Environment
title: Landslides and Mudflows
description: A quick, practical guide to Landslides and Mudflows.

hook.text: After a wildfire, the next rain doesn't soak in. It slides down the hill carrying everything.

buildup.text: Saturated soil on steep slopes becomes heavy and unstable. Gravity does the rest.

discovery.text: Deforestation multiplies landslide risk. Tree roots are the glue that holds hillsides together.

twist.text: A single landslide in Colombia in 2017 killed 300 people in minutes while they slept.

climax.text: As extreme rainfall events increase, landslide-prone areas face growing danger each year.

punchline.text: Mountains look permanent. Heavy rain can prove otherwise.

quiz.question: Why does deforestation increase landslide risk?
options: Tree roots hold soil in place on slopes
Forests block wind that causes slides

details.summary: Landslides occur when saturated earth loses integrity on slopes and collapses downhill, often triggered by intense rainfall, earthquakes, or deforestation. Mudflows carrying boulders and debris can reach speeds over 50 km/h and bury communities without warning.
details.whyItMatters: Climate change increases landslide risk through more intense rainfall and permafrost thaw. Deforestation on slopes removes the root systems that hold soil in place.
takeaways: Heavy rainfall is the most common landslide trigger worldwide
Deforested slopes are far more susceptible to sliding
Landslides kill thousands of people annually, mostly in developing nations

faq.question: Why are developing countries more affected by landslides?
faq.answer: Dense populations living on steep, deforested hillsides with poor drainage and no early warning systems face the worst outcomes. Informal settlements in tropical mountain regions are especially vulnerable during intense monsoon rainfall.

faq.question: Can landslides be predicted?
faq.answer: Rainfall thresholds that trigger slides in specific geologies can be established, and some areas use sensors and satellite monitoring. However, the exact timing and location of individual slides remain difficult to predict, making evacuation planning essential.
